segments.voice: Yesterday: Uttararamacharita, and the poets' three choices. Bhavabhuti rewrote the ending toward reunion, Kamban closed at the crowning, and Valmiki's text kept the earth opening. Did you notice someone who loves what you love, arguing with you? Today, the two sides of the argument itself. Day six hundred sixty-eight.

A Ramayana play has ended, and a family is still at the dinner table. Someone's uncle says Rama did the right thing: a king belongs to his people first. Someone's aunt puts down her spoon and says Sita did nothing wrong, and she was sent away pregnant into a forest. A teenager asks why nobody asked Sita. Each of them is drawing on the tradition. Tables like that one are part of how the story lives. Today we hear the strongest form of each side, and Sita's own words from the text.
screen: `AFTER THE PLAY, AT THE TABLE.` → `HE WAS A KING FIRST.` → `SHE DID NOTHING WRONG.`

segments.voice: The first side rests on a Sanskrit idea: rajadharma, the duty of a king. In this reading, Rama's private life is not his own. A king who keeps what he loves while his people lose faith in him has failed the kingdom, so Rama gives up the thing dearest to him and suffers for it. The poem does show him suffering. Those who read it this way see the exile as a terrible sacrifice made by both of them, and they honor it as such. The second side starts from Sita. She was tested by fire already, in the war book, and found pure. She is pregnant. She is sent away without a hearing, by a husband who knows she's innocent. Readers on this side, devotees of Rama among them, say this is a wound in the story, and they won't pretend it isn't. Some honor Sita as the true center of the poem. And then there are Sita's own words. When Lakshmana leaves her at the Ganga, Valmiki gives her a message to send back. She says she knows she is blameless. She says she won't grieve for herself. She tells him she carries his child. And she asks Rama to care for the people of the city as he would his own brothers. There is no shouting in it, and a great deal of dignity. Women's songs in several Indian languages keep Sita's side alive, singing her grief in the forest. Both readings are inside the faith. Neither has won.
screen: `RAJADHARMA: THE KING'S DUTY.` · `A SACRIFICE MADE BY BOTH.` · `SITA: BLAMELESS, PREGNANT, UNHEARD.` · `HER OWN MESSAGE BACK TO RAMA.` · then, large: `BOTH READINGS ARE INSIDE THE FAITH.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath find its own pace. Think of a real disagreement in your life, with someone you care about. For one breath, argue their side as well as you can, as if you believed it. For the next breath, your own side. Go back and forth a few times, slowly, without picking a winner. Then let both go and simply breathe. The bell holds the time.
Rajadharma. The king's duty, on one side; Sita's innocence on the other; both held by people who love the story.
Your line: both readings are inside the faith. Today, in one disagreement, say the other person's best point back to them before you make yours. Day six hundred sixty-eight.

howItsDone: Hindu teachers, storytellers and families discuss Sita's exile openly: some defend Rama's choice as a king's duty, some grieve it as a wrong done to Sita, and women's folk songs in several languages sing her side.

original.note: Sanskrit rājadharma: rāja (king) + dharma (duty, right order). the duty a ruler owes the people.

trapdoor: what you thought: either Rama was right or the story is wrong.
what it means: devotees hold both readings, the king's duty and Sita's innocence, inside the faith.
what a scholar hears: rajadharma is a major theme of Sanskrit epic and law texts, and Sita's message at the Ganga is one of the places the Uttara Kanda gives her own voice.
